> We all save time and money with XSLT.

Ah, but you see, Google doesn't and that appears to be what actually matters here.

Reminder that Google is a multi-*trillion* dollar company so I find financial arguments against maintaining a long-standing feature to ring extremely hollow. Same goes for Microsoft and Apple.

The only maintainer where this argument would carry any weight is Mozilla but, as far as I can tell, no one from Mozilla has chimed in on this (correct me if I am wrong), though I would *guess* based on [Mozilla's other positions](https://mozilla.github.io/standards-positions/), they would actually be against this despite being a much smaller organization.

Some folks from Mozilla has expressed the support for trying to remove XSLT in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11523. Major browser vendors are unanimous in this regard. None of us want to maintain XSLT support in the browser engine if we don't have to. This ultimately comes down to whether removing the support for XSLT is Web compatible or not. If it's still widely used as some proponents have suggested, then we can't remove it.

> Some folks from Mozilla has expressed the support for trying to remove XSLT in #11523. Major browser vendors are unanimous in this regard. None of us want to maintain XSLT support in the browser engine

Who said it has to be in the browser engine and why would it affect the standard? Is there a problem with the XSLT standard itself?
We're discussing removing XSLT from the web standard because the implementation in browsers that are major (today...) is bad or inconvenient.. now it is, but it doesn't have to be.

XSLT support could well be via a built-in (or installed by default) extension that would have no special permissions at all and would only use stable web APIs. XSLT 1.0 is itself stable, so why is it such a big problem for browser vendors?

> XSLT support could well be via a built-in (or installed by default) extension that would have no special permissions at all and would only use stable web APIs. XSLT 1.0 is itself stable, so why is it such a big problem for browser vendors?

Because XSLT is implemented using a library such as `libxslt` which isn't well maintained. It's frequently a source of remote-code-execution security vulnerabilities in browser engines so real users are suffering the consequence of it being not well maintained. Now, browser vendors could alternatively re-implement XSLT using a memory safe language like Swift or Rust to deal with this situation if it's worth the engineering effort. However, the rough consensus among browser vendors is that it is not worth the effort since the usage of XSLT is so low compared to other web platform features.

Transpiling libxlst to WASM or adopting a JS implementation of XSLT, as suggested by some people on the original issue, might be an interesting alternative if it can be achieved without much engineering effort and there are enough XSLT usage on the web such that we want to maintain the support for foreseeable future.

> if it can be achieved without much engineering effort and there are enough XSLT usage on the web such that we want to maintain the support for foreseeable future.

The polyfill for the JS API is _already written_.. even by the author of that original issue!

I'm sure other people could volunteer to wrap this into a browser extension (which only uses **stable** web APIs) that could also handle XML files with `xml-stylesheet` processing instruction opened in the browser. This way we'd not break anything.

Then, given that:
- that browser extension would only use stable Web APIs
- XSLT is itself stable (security would no longer be a concern)

what's there to maintain, precisely?

Even considering libxslt, how many of those commits fix bugs other than security and are not build-related/libxml-related changes? 
https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/libxslt/-/commits/master/libxslt

Normally I'm the last person to suggest we might solve the problem with AI, but when it comes to a simple browser extension, then...

> > if it can be achieved without much engineering effort and there are enough XSLT usage on the web such that we want to maintain the support for foreseeable future.
> 
> The polyfill for the JS API is _already written_.. even by the author of that original issue!
> 
> I'm sure other people could volunteer to wrap this into a browser extension (which only uses **stable** web APIs) that could also handle XML files with `xml-stylesheet` processing instruction opened in the browser. This way we'd not break anything.

Right, we need to hook it up with the rest of web browser. I'm not sure if writing such a browser extension is easy or not. It could be someone's weekend project. It could be someone's full time job for a few weeks or months. Integrating such an alternative implementation with the rest of a browser engine is probably not trivial but probably much less work than rewriting `libxslt` in a memory safe language so might be still a good alternative.

So the question is really whether supporting XSLT is essential for the Web compatibility or not today. If it is, then these alternative approaches seem attractive. If it is not, then removing it altogether might be the answer although I get that people don't like (their favorite) features getting removed.

It is no secret that XSLT enables pure XML sites.

I'm just a user, completely unaffiliated with any of the browser makers. And if you've seen my post in https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11563#issuecomment-3190981127, you'll know that I'm very much against removing XSLT.

That being said, there's no conspiracy here whatsoever. No one is trying to end the “open web”, or break small non-commercial sites, or push anyone towards some proprietary alternative. And I agree with most of the comments that either “security” or “lack of use” on their own would be poor reasons to remove XSLT, together they make sense: the current XSLT implementation _is_ a security risk, so it needs to be changed, but _if_ nobody is using it, then there's no reason to put in the effort for a new solution (like a built-in polyfill or the implementation in Rust).

Also, keep in mind that the browser development teams used to be larger, but after layoffs, they're now smaller, which means that the teams need to find _something_ to cut. And yes, Google/Apple/Microsoft are multi-billion-dollar companies and certainly _could_ afford to increase funding for browser development, but that's completely irrelevant here—development funding is decided by executive management, and the developers who are graciously communicating with us here have no control over their own resources. And trust me, I can promise you that every single developer here feels the same frustration at the lack of funding, even more than us—we see the lack of funding as less-common features being deprecated, but they see the lack of funding as their colleagues being laid off.

So to any of the browsers developers reading, I hope that you'll reconsider removing XSLT from the web platform, and I'll be disappointed if you choose to remove it, but I'll understand it if you choose remove it and to prioritize other technologies instead. And to anyone else reading, please remember that the browser developers here are real humans, who actually took the time to hear us out, and attacking them just makes it even less likely that they'll listen to us.
